# French multi-word expressions: the patterns. Hand-curated — not generated by
# dictgen.
#
# Format: one pattern per line, `#` comments ignored. What each one *means* is
# in `phrases.<meta>.txt`, joined on the pattern — the same split `lex.txt` and
# `gloss.<meta>.txt` make, for the same reason. Which phrases exist is a fact
# about French; what they mean is a fact about a pair of languages.
#
# A pattern is a sequence of slots matched against consecutive tokens. Each
# slot matches a token's **root** or its normalised surface, so a pattern whose
# head inflects is written in the citation form (`avoir raison` catches `a
# raison`, `as raison`, `avais raison`) and an invariant phrase is written just
# as it is read (`en fait`).
#
# **Elision is a token boundary here, so it is a slot boundary too.** The pack's
# tokeniser splits `s'il` into `s'` and `il`, and the frequency corpus behind it
# does the same, so `s'` is an ordinary headword and the pattern is written
# `s' il vous plaît` — four slots, spaces where the tokeniser cuts. A pattern
# written `s'il vous plaît` has a first slot no token can ever equal, and would
# silently never fire. `qu' est-ce que` is the same rule: `est-ce` is one token
# because the hyphen does not cut, and `qu'` is another because the apostrophe
# does.
#
# There is no frequency data behind these — the rank list is unigram — which is
# why a phrase carries no band and never enters the band histogram. See NOTICE
# at the repo root.
#
# ## What belongs here
#
# Only phrases where the word-by-word reading misleads. Transparent
# prepositional phrases (`près de`, `à côté de`) are out: an underline over a
# phrase the reader can decode is noise that makes the ones that matter easier
# to ignore.
#
# ## Every pattern here was measured before it shipped
#
# `npm run measure:phrase-fit -- --lang fr` runs the shipping matcher over a
# subtitle sample and reports which patterns fire and on which surfaces. **No
# count from that run is recorded in this file**: the phrase list carries no
# frequency data, which is what keeps it out of the band histogram and off the
# licence of `ranks.txt`. The numbers are in `tools/measure/README.md`.
#
# Two patterns were rewritten because the check showed the *shape* was wrong,
# not the phrase:
#
#   - `se rendre compte` catches only the third person, because `me`, `te` and
#     `nous` are their own roots and never fold to `se`. Written `rendre compte`
#     it catches all of them, and that is what ships.
#   - `s' en aller` misses `je m'en vais` for the same reason; `en aller` does
#     not.
#
# `se mettre à` keeps its reflexive, and that is the counter-example: bare
# `mettre à` fires half again as often and most of the extra is literal — `mis à
# jour`, `mettre à la poubelle`. Dropping a clitic is a fix only where the
# remainder is not itself an ordinary phrase.
#
# Three more patterns exist because the corpus puts a word inside the phrase or
# in front of it that the obvious pattern has no room for: `pas la peine` is
# what `valoir la peine` becomes under negation and is the commoner of the two,
# and `avoir du mal` and `faire du mal` are two different idioms sharing one
# noun, neither reachable from `mal` alone.
#
# ## The negation is deliberately not here
#
# `ne … pas` and its four siblings are the reason the gap slot exists, and they
# are still carried by the parenthetical glosses on `pas`, `plus`, `rien` and
# `personne`. Two things argue for leaving them out until the shape has been
# reviewed in the running app. `ne * pas` opens on more than one token in a
# hundred: underlining the ordinary negation of the language is not annotating
# an expression, it is drawing a box around French grammar. And `ne * que` — the
# one that is genuinely non-compositional, "only" — cannot be told from a
# negated verb with a `que` complement by a wide gap, so it catches `n'ont pas
# dit que`. The narrow gap (`ne ? que`) is clean but drops every `ne le fait
# que`. Which of those a reader is better served by is a judgement to make with
# text on the screen.
